arcs.title: The Book wakes
arcs.pitch: The Book's ledger, region by region. Each mythic you bring it is a name it already knew, and each region shows a little more of why something is waking the cryptids. What the Book is stays the owner's to write; these beats only point at it.

beats.title: Item 1
beats.text: The two greys drop you in the pines at Batsto with a book that talks. Its first demand is written in rust over the printed page: every cryptid on earth, start with three. The rust on the page is the same colour as the bog iron in the streams.

beats.title: A page already written
beats.text: When the Jersey Devil's ink holds, its page is not blank. A faded entry is already there, in the same rust hand, older than the Leeds house. The Book says nothing about it. Owner writes what the Book says, if anything.

beats.title: Someone writes back
beats.text: Inside the Radio Quiet Zone, where no phone works, the Book's hand moves on a page you did not open. A line is added under the last demand, in a hand that is not the Book's. The Office's agents are at Green Bank for the same silence.

beats.title: The warning on the pier
beats.text: At the Silver Bridge's old piers, Mothman stands on the far bank and does not fight. In the legend it comes before a disaster. It looks at the Book, not at you. The next section's stone is where you fight it.

beats.title: Margin notes, 1910
beats.text: A copy of Cox's Fearsome Creatures of the Lumberwoods, left in a camp stove, has notes in its margins in the Book's own rust hand: the Book was carried through the lumber camps before. Dr. Vale wants the copy; the Book wants you to burn it.

beats.title: The torn page
beats.text: In the corner of the 1977 Champ photograph there is a pale square on the water: a page. The Book has a stub where a leaf was cut. Champ's water holds it; beating Champ lets you dive for it.

beats.title: The page comes home
beats.text: The wet page goes back in at the stub and the Book reads it out: a list of names, crossed through, region by region. Owner writes what the page says.

beats.title: What the ash holds
beats.text: The 1980 ash under the Mount St. Helens forest has rust-coloured flecks in it, and the wild ones roam thickest where the ash lies deepest. Dr. Vale's ash cores say the flecks are not from the volcano. The land itself is waking them.

beats.title: The greys come back
beats.text: Lights over Roswell, and the same two greys, very nervous, land in a dry wash. They did not lose the Book: they left it, because of what came after it. They will not say what. They ask if it has been fed.

beats.title: The curse passes
beats.text: In the legend the rougarou's curse passes to whoever draws its blood. After the bayou's mythic is bound, the hand that writes the demands starts to look like yours. Owner writes the turn.

beats.title: The last page of the north
beats.text: With the Ozark Howler bound, every North American mythic is in the Book. It turns to a new block of pages, all blank but one name, and points south over the gulf. The road needs a swimmer.
beats.opens: the south: regions 9-16, with a swimmer in the line-up

arcs.title: Gary's documentary
arcs.pitch: Gary narrates the found tapes, always one region ahead of you and always just missing the shot. His tapes get stranger and closer, until you meet him at Fouke, where the old drive-in still shows a monster film.

beats.title: Gary and the cedar water
beats.text: The first Gary tape: cedar water, tannins, 'the water just moved'. Nobody knows who Gary is; the Lamplighters have heard of a man with a camera.

beats.title: Hold the shot
beats.text: Gary at the New River Gorge bridge: something on the far cliff waves. If you go to that cliff, his tripod marks are still in the moss and there is a dropped lens cap with a name scratched on it.

beats.title: The tripod at Niagara
beats.text: Gary's tripod stands on the Canadian side of the falls, still running. The tape in it is of you, from the day before. He is ahead of you on purpose.

beats.title: Footprints at White Sands
beats.text: At White Sands the gypsum keeps tracks for days. Gary's boot prints walk beside something with three toes, then the boot prints run.

beats.title: Gary in person
beats.text: In Fouke, Arkansas, Gary is editing his film in a motel room. He is not a hunter; he wants one true shot so people believe him. Show him the Book, or don't. Either way he joins the believers' fire at the Howl-Back Club's ridge.

arcs.title: The last bearer
arcs.pitch: The rust thumbprint on every page belongs to someone. Their trail runs through lumber camps, a ghost town and a bayou: a hat, a field guide, a pirogue. Who they were is the owner's to write.

beats.title: The hat in the pine
beats.text: Ong's Hat is named for a hat thrown into a pine that never came down. It is still up there. Climb for it and the hat band has a rust thumbprint inside.

beats.title: The camp ledger
beats.text: The logging camp's 1908 ledger has one man paid in cryptids: hodag, squonk, agropelter, the Book's own starters, with the same thumbprint by his mark.

beats.title: A pirogue in the cypress
beats.text: In Big Cypress a sunk pirogue has a tin box under its seat. In it, the bearer's last note. Owner writes the note.

arcs.title: Letters between the fires
arcs.pitch: The eight believer groups write to each other but never meet. Carry their letters camp to camp along the road and, at the end, they hold their first convention at the Howl-Back Club's ridge. Each letter makes the next camp trust you sooner.

beats.title: A letter in foil
beats.text: The Hatters of Ong's Hat give you a letter wrapped in tin foil for the Porchlight Vigil, 'so the mothmen can't read it'.

beats.title: A moth-wing seal
beats.text: The Porchlight Vigil reads the letter by porch light and writes back, sealed with a moth wing, to the Backwards Lodge.

beats.title: Written backwards
beats.text: The Backwards Lodge answers in mirror writing. Hold it to your lamp at the Frog Watch's landing to read it.

beats.title: A wet letter
beats.text: The Frog Watch dry the letter by their torches and add a pressed frog (rubber) for the Blurry Society.

beats.title: A blurry photograph
beats.text: The Blurry Society send their best photograph, which shows nothing at all, to the Antler Choir.

beats.title: A sung letter
beats.text: The Antler Choir can't write; they sing the answer, and you carry the tune to the Thirteen Counters.

beats.title: Thirteen beans
beats.text: The Thirteen Counters send a jar of beans, counted. Don't spill it on the way to the Ozarks.

beats.title: The first convention
beats.text: All eight groups at the Howl-Back Club's ridge, one big fire, hats, capes, mirrors, goggles, waders, antlers, beans and earmuffs. They tell you where a cryptid you don't hold yet roams, in every region at once.
beats.opens: every believer's hint at once, on the big map

arcs.title: Evenings in the east
arcs.pitch: One place, one evening each: a fire tower, a flooded bog, a logging train, a feud, a county fair, a portage.

beats.title: Fire tower watch
beats.text: The warden at Apple Pie Hill's fire tower needs a night watcher. From the cab you can see Philadelphia's glow and Atlantic City's. Mark three lights moving over the pines that are not planes; the third one is the Jersey Devil, and its route shows the 1909 trail.

beats.title: Flood the bog
beats.text: At harvest a grower floods the cranberry bog so the ripe berries float. Open the sluice gates in order. When the red rises, something heavy is moving under it.

beats.title: The Shay up the grade
beats.text: Ride the geared Shay locomotive from Cass up to Bald Knob. Halfway, the snallygaster drops on the train. Fight on the flatcar while the grade gets steeper.

beats.title: Feud lines
beats.text: Two families on either side of the Tug Fork both say they saw the wampus cat first, and both want it shot. Walk both banks, read the tracks, and find it saw them.

beats.title: The fair hodag
beats.text: Rhinelander's fair wants Shepard's 1896 wired wooden hodag rebuilt. Find the parts in town. On fair night a real one comes to look at it.

beats.title: Portage
beats.text: In the Boundary Waters you carry a canoe lake to lake over the portage trails. Every portage has a snapped spruce on it, snapped from the inside: a splintercat's trail.

arcs.title: Evenings in the west
arcs.pitch: A fallen giant, a missing reel, an island with no cars, a wolf count, a cave of bats, a crater survey.

beats.title: Count the rings
beats.text: Toby Reyes needs the rings of a fallen Sitka spruce in the Hoh counted before dark. Every ring has a year; one ring is scorched in a year with no fire on record.

beats.title: The missing frames
beats.text: The 1967 Bluff Creek film runs about a minute. A collector says there were more frames, cut and lost. Find three cans of film at the creek's old camps.

beats.title: No cars on Mackinac
beats.text: Cars have been banned on Mackinac Island since 1898. The Office's sedan is stuck at the ferry dock. Deliver their forms by bicycle before the last boat.

beats.title: The wolf count
beats.text: Wolves and moose on Isle Royale have been counted every winter since 1958, the longest study of its kind. Help the count from a snow camp; one set of tracks is not a wolf's.

beats.title: The bat flight
beats.text: Summer dusk at Carlsbad Caverns: hundreds of thousands of Mexican free-tailed bats pour out of the cave mouth. Sit in the amphitheatre with the ranger. One shape in the swarm is far too big.

beats.title: Crater survey
beats.text: Meteor Crater is about 1.2 km across and 50,000 years old. Walk the rim with a survey stake and place five marks. The fourth mark is already there, in rust.

arcs.title: Evenings in the south
arcs.pitch: A faith healer, a smugglers' bay, a diamond field, a storm chase.

beats.title: The traiteur
beats.text: In Acadiana a traiteur, a Cajun folk healer, treats your knocked-out beast with a prayer said under the breath. It works. She won't take money; she asks for one true story about the rougarou.

beats.title: By pirogue to Barataria
beats.text: Jean Lafitte's smugglers used the Barataria marshes. Pole a pirogue through the cuts at night with Old Dutch's cousin, lamps out, past the Office's boat.

beats.title: Finders keepers
beats.text: At Crater of Diamonds State Park you keep any stone you find. Dig in the ploughed field after rain, when the stones shine. One of them is warm.

beats.title: Storm chase
beats.text: Ride with a storm spotter under a supercell in Tornado Alley. Call the hail size and the wall cloud. In the roar a howl answers, and the spotter writes it down as wind.

arcs.title: Tools of the road
arcs.pitch: What you carry decides where you can go: a lamp for the night, a radio for rumours, a canoe for the lakes, a bicycle for the island, a second pen for the Book. Each comes from someone you meet, at a level.

beats.title: Lit fires
beats.text: Every campfire you light is a rest and a place to travel back to.

beats.title: The lamp
beats.text: Wren Ashby gives you a Lamplighters' lamp. With it lit, the wild ones keep back a little after dark, and the dim lights on the night paths show you the way.
beats.opens: walking the night paths by lamp

beats.title: Sparrow's radio
beats.text: Pip gives you a radio tuned to the Lamplighters' channel. Sightings come in as rumours and show on the big map. In the Quiet Zone it hisses.

beats.title: The canoe
beats.text: After the portage, the canoe is yours. Lakes and slow rivers in the north woods become roads.

beats.title: The second pen
beats.text: The Book grows a second pen loop in its spine and wants it filled. With two pens, a bind gets a fourth try.

beats.title: The canteen
beats.text: A rancher outside Roswell fills you a canvas canteen. Without it the deep desert in the heat of the day wears your line-up down; with it you can cross the flats at noon.
beats.opens: crossing the open desert by day

beats.title: The airboat
beats.text: After the traiteur's story, her nephew lends you his airboat. The sawgrass and the open marsh become fast roads, loud enough that the wild ones hear you coming.
beats.opens: fast travel over marsh and sawgrass

beats.title: The float trip
beats.text: An outfitter on the Buffalo River rents you a jon boat. Float the river from bluff to bluff; each gravel bar you camp on is a fire to travel back to.

areas.feel: Flat, sandy, hushed and endless: pitch pine and scrub oak to every edge, tea-brown rivers, white sugar-sand roads, and ghost towns where iron was once made from the bogs.

world.what: Batsto Village: the ironmaster's mansion, the sawmill, the gristmill and the workers' cottages along the lake, built of local stone and cedar.
Apple Pie Hill's steel fire tower with a cab on top, the only high point for miles, the Batona Trail passing its foot.
Sugar-sand roads: white, soft and deep-rutted, with the pines close on both sides and puddles the colour of tea.
Cranberry bogs in rows behind low dykes and sluice gates, flooded red at harvest.
Atsion Lake: cedar water the colour of strong tea, a sand beach and a dock, white cedars dark round the far shore.
Rivers and streams the colour of tea from the cedar swamps, running out dark into the bay.
Short, crooked pitch pines, none much over ten metres, standing open over waist-high scrub oak and huckleberry.
Atlantic white cedar, dark and close, only where the ground is wet: along the streams and round the lakes.
Pitch pine bark blackened by old fires, with new tufts of needles growing straight from the trunk.
The Pine Barrens tree frog (green with a lavender stripe), northern pine snakes, deer, turkey vultures over the plains.
Summer thunderstorms that roll in at dusk.
Spring smoke from controlled burns lying low in the pines.
Whip-poor-wills calling at dusk, the tree frog's nasal quonk, thunder over the pines.
Wind in pitch pine needles, sand squeaking underfoot.
Pineys: old families who cut cedar, pick berries and know every sand road by name; the Hatters of Ong's Hat at the first fire.
Bog iron, glass works and charcoal pits of the 1700s and 1800s; cannonballs for the Revolution cast at Batsto.
Cedar shingles, wood-fired glass, cranberry scoops, a diner on the highway with a neon sign that hums.
Two soft wheel ruts down every sugar-sand road, packed darker than the loose white sand of the crown.

areas.feel: Steep green ridges folded close, fog in every hollow at dawn, coal towns down by the rivers, and radio silence around a giant dish.

world.what: The New River Gorge Bridge, a rust-brown steel arch 876 feet over the river, with rafts far below.
The Green Bank telescope, a white dish as wide as a football field, rising over farm fields.
Seneca Rocks: a thin fin of pale sandstone standing up from the trees.
The McClintic igloos: concrete bunkers half-buried in grass in the woods, doors rusted shut.
Rhododendron and mountain laurel thickets on the slopes, red spruce on the high knobs, tulip poplars in the coves.
Black bears, wild turkeys, timber rattlesnakes on warm rocks, luna moths at the porch light.
Morning valley fog that burns off by ten; cold at night on the knobs even in summer.
Creek water over rocks, a far coal train, a banjo on a porch, the hum of the ridge after dark.
The Porchlight Vigil in moth capes; coal families; whitewater guides; the Office's sedan that won't start.
The 1859 raid at Harpers Ferry, the Hatfield and McCoy feud, the Silver Bridge's fall in 1967.
Quilts on porch rails, moonshine stills in the hollows, company-town houses all alike.

areas.feel: Lakes beyond counting, dark spruce and white birch, the cold edge of Superior, and the tall tales of the lumber camps told round a stove.

world.what: A logging camp: bunkhouse, cook shack, a saw pit and a stack of white pine logs stamped with the company's mark.
The giant Paul Bunyan and Babe the blue ox statues standing in a lakeside town.
Boundary Waters portages: worn trails between lakes, a canoe rest, granite shores.
Lake Superior's shore of basalt and agate pebbles, cold clear water, a lighthouse on a cliff.
White pine, black spruce bogs, paper birch, tamarack gone gold in autumn, blueberries on the burns.
Loons on every lake, moose in the shallows, timber wolves, black flies in June.
Deep snow and lake-effect squalls in winter; northern lights on clear cold nights.
The loon's wail across water at night, ice booming on a frozen lake, the axe and the crosscut saw.
The Backwards Lodge with mirrors on their headbands; old lumberjacks; Ojibwe rice harvesters on the lakes (setting, told with care).
The white pine logging boom of 1870-1910; Eugene Shepard's hodag hoax of 1893.
Peaveys and pike poles, birchbark canoes, wool plaid coats, a cook shack's tin plates.

areas.feel: Green on green: moss over everything, giant trees, mist off the sea, a volcano with its side blown out.

world.what: The Hoh rain forest's Hall of Mosses: big-leaf maples hung with club moss, nurse logs with saplings in a row.
Mount St. Helens' blast zone: grey pumice plain, standing dead trees all fallen one way, the crater open to the north.
Multnomah Falls: a two-tier fall with a stone footbridge across between them.
Crater Lake: deep blue water in a caldera, Wizard Island's cone in it.
Sitka spruce, western red cedar and Douglas fir, sword ferns, banana slugs, Roosevelt elk.
Salmon running up the rivers in autumn, bald eagles on the snags, ravens.
Rain most days, soft and steady; sea fog in the morning; snow on the volcano tops all year.
Drip from every branch, the raven's knock, surf on Cape Flattery, a wood knock in the distance with no one there.
The Blurry Society in smeared goggles; loggers and tree planters; the Sts'ailes hold the sásq'ets as real: setting, asked first, never a fighter.
The 1958 Bluff Creek tracks; the 1967 film; the 1980 eruption.
Plaster track casts, cedar plank houses (setting), fire lookouts, a coffee stand by the highway.

areas.feel: Water as wide as a sea, lighthouses and ferries, an island with no cars, and a long lake between mountains where something keeps surfacing.

world.what: Niagara Falls: the horseshoe curve of the Canadian falls, spray rising, a boat in the mist below.
Mackinac Island: white Victorian hotels, horse carts, bicycles, fudge shops, no cars.
Lake Champlain: a long narrow lake between the Adirondacks and the Green Mountains, Valcour Island in it.
Lighthouses on every point, and ore freighters 300 m long passing slowly.
Moose and wolves on Isle Royale, lake sturgeon, gulls, sand dunes on Lake Michigan's east shore.
Gales in November that sink ships; lake-effect snow; still summer evenings with the water like glass.
Foghorns, horse hooves on Mackinac's streets, waves on shingle, a freighter's horn.
The Frog Watch in waders with torches; ferry crews; lighthouse keepers' families.
The 1977 Champ photograph; the Battle of Valcour Island in 1776; shipwrecks of the lakes.
Fudge, birch-bark souvenirs, lake boats, a lighthouse lens of brass and glass.

areas.feel: Red rock and white sand under a huge sky, saguaros like people, a canyon a mile deep, and lights in the sky everyone has a story about.

world.what: White Sands: gypsum dunes so white they look like snow, ripples on every crest.
The Grand Canyon rim at sunset, layered rock in red and cream, the river too far down to hear.
Roswell's main street with alien shop signs, and the dry ranch land outside town.
Meteor Crater's rim and bowl, about 1.2 km across.
Saguaro and cholla, creosote bush, Joshua trees; roadrunners, coyotes, jackrabbits, rattlesnakes.
Monsoon thunderstorms in July and August, flash floods in dry washes, very cold clear nights.
Coyotes at night, wind over sand, a far freight train, the click of cooling rock after sunset.
The Antler Choir round their fire; ranchers; road-trippers at a motel pool. The skinwalker is held sacred: never shown.
The 1947 Roswell report; the 1995 Puerto Rico goat deaths that named the chupacabra; Douglas, Wyoming's jackalopes.
Neon motel signs, adobe walls, turquoise and silver (setting), a jackalope mount over the bar.

areas.feel: Slow black water, cypress knees, Spanish moss in the heat, Cajun French on the radio, and a river of grass to the edge of the sky.

world.what: Atchafalaya Basin: cypress-tupelo swamp, a stilt camp on the water, a boat landing with a bait shop.
The Everglades' river of grass: sawgrass to the horizon, tree islands, a boardwalk.
Barataria's marsh cuts and shell middens.
Bald cypress with knees, Spanish moss, water hyacinth; alligators, herons, egrets, roseate spoonbills, crawfish.
Heavy wet heat, an afternoon storm every day in summer, hurricanes in the fall.
Bullfrogs and cicadas, an airboat far off, a Cajun accordion and fiddle from a dance hall.
The Thirteen Counters on their jetty; Cajun families; shrimpers; the traiteur.
The Acadians' arrival after 1755; Lafitte's smugglers; the rougarou of Lent.
Pirogues, crawfish traps, a gumbo pot, Mardi Gras masks, a bottle tree.

areas.feel: Old worn hills full of caves and springs, giving way west to flat open plains and enormous storms.

world.what: The Buffalo River's tall limestone bluffs over a clear green river, gravel bars to camp on.
Hot Springs' bathhouse row, and steaming water coming out of the hill.
A Route 66 stretch: an old gas station, a motel court, a diner, a roadside giant.
Caves and sinkholes in the karst, cold air breathing out of the cave mouths.
Oak-hickory forest, dogwood in spring; elk on the Buffalo, armadillos, bison on the Wichita grassland.
Supercell thunderstorms and tornadoes in spring, hail, then hot still summers with fireflies.
A tornado siren, cicadas, a fiddle at a pickin' night, rain on a tin roof.
The Howl-Back Club with earmuffs and tin cups; storm spotters; float-trip outfitters.
The Fouke Monster sightings of the 1970s and the 1972 film; the old Route 66.
Jon boats, quilts, fiddles, a diamond sieve at the crater park.
